module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Green's Open Problem 44

*References:*
- [Gr24] [Ben Green's 100 Open Problems](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.44)
- [Er80] Erdős, Paul. "A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory."
  Annals of Discrete Mathematics 6 (1980): 89-115.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Green44

open scoped Nat

/--
Sieve $[N]$ by removing half the residue classes mod $p_i$, for primes
$2 \leqslant p_1 < p_2 < \dots < p_{1000} < N^{9/10}$. Does the remaining set have size at most
$\frac{1}{10} N$?

We interpret "half the residue classes" as $\lfloor p_i / 2 \rfloor$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem green_44 :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (N : ℕ) (p : Fin 1000 → ℕ) (A : (i : Fin 1000) → Finset (ZMod (p i))),
      let remaining := (Finset.Icc 1 N).filter (fun x => ∀ i, (x : ZMod (p i)) ∉ A i)
      (∀ i, (p i).Prime) →
      StrictMono p →
      (p 999) ^ 10 < N ^ 9 →
      (∀ i, (A i).card = (p i) / 2) →
      10 * remaining.card ≤ N := by
  sorry

/-- The answer is affirmative if the primes are all less than $N^{1/2}$, by the large sieve. [Gr24] -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem green_44.variants.less_than_sqrt :
    ∀ (N : ℕ) (p : Fin 1000 → ℕ) (A : (i : Fin 1000) → Finset (ZMod (p i))),
      let remaining := (Finset.Icc 1 N).filter (fun x => ∀ i, (x : ZMod (p i)) ∉ A i)
      (∀ i, (p i).Prime) →
      StrictMono p →
      (p 999) ^ 2 < N →
      (∀ i, (A i).card = (p i) / 2) →
      10 * remaining.card ≤ N := by
  sorry

end Green44

reformulations.difference: The source bounds every prime by √N and the remaining cardinality by N/10; Lean bounds only the last prime using `(p 999)^2 < N` and writes `10 * remaining.card ≤ N`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: StrictMono makes p 999 the largest of the 1000 primes. For nonnegative p and N, p² < N iff p < √N, and multiplication by the positive constant 10 converts the cardinality bound exactly. These component equivalences were proved in the scratch file.

sources_consulted: https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.44 — Problem 44 and comments, pp. 22–23; notation on p. 2.
https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1980-03.pdf — Paul Erdős, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory, §6, Problem 3, p. 107.
https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/ — identifies the current problem-list update as January 2026.
could_not_verify: Green44.green_44: I could not establish whether Green's fixed-1000 formulation is intended to include an implicit 'for sufficiently large N' restriction. Problem 44 does not explicitly specify one; Erdős's original passage instead quantifies an unspecified k depending on two parameters. The literal universal reading matches the Lean but admits the counterexample above. Source clarification is needed before identifying the N quantifier as a confirmed defect.
review.notes:
No confirmed discrepancy from the cited wording was established. The square-root variant matches the source, including its solved status. Prime hypotheses exclude ZMod 0 and ZMod 1; the indexing, interval, residue casts, rounding, and numerical bounds were checked.

Important caveat: I proved the negation of the main theorem's universal RHS in /workspace/review/counterexample.lean, without using either imported conjecture or any sorry. Take N = 100000 and the first 1000 primes in [20003,31500] (there are 1127, checked computationally in Lean). For each p, delete residues {p - floor(p/2), ..., p - 1}. Exactly floor(p/2) classes are deleted, every integer 1 through 10001 survives, and p_max^10 < N^9. Thus 10 * remaining.card > N. The finite prime-count certificate uses native_decide.

This deserves maintainer attention, but the source uses essentially the same wording and the answer slot is unfixed. A negative answer to that literal question is not by itself evidence of a misformalization. Neither cited source records this resolution, so I have not reported a source-backed status mismatch or asserted that adding an eventual quantifier repairs the intended problem.
